themes.name: How should trademark law address search diversion, algorithmic filtering, and brand use in online environments?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether digital search systems and online intermediaries change how marks convey information, divert consumers, or create actionable confusion.

themes.name: How should trademark law determine the geographic scope of rights for unregistered marks used through the Internet?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether traditional territorial and locally fragmented trademark rights remain appropriate when online use creates national or global commercial reach.

themes.name: When do unconventional designs, product features, or digital identifiers function as trademarks and acquire protectable distinctiveness?
themes.definition: This question examines whether nontraditional matter, including trade dress and technologically mediated identifiers, performs a source-identifying function and satisfies secondary-meaning requirements.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect the associative and persuasive meanings of brands beyond their literal source-identifying content?
themes.definition: This question asks whether law should recognize trademarks as repositories of reputation, quality, cultural meaning, and brand differentiation or limit protection to conventional origin information.

themes.name: Does expanded trademark protection improperly restrict competition, secondary markets, or competitors’ use of necessary product and brand identifiers?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether exclusive control over marks and related features creates barriers to entry, intrabrand competition, resale, consumer access, or functional communication.

themes.name: What legal mechanisms can curb abusive trademark enforcement without weakening legitimate protection against infringement?
themes.definition: This question concerns trademark bullying, overclaiming, and unjustified threats, including whether clearer defenses, procedural reforms, or alternative remedies can reduce chilling effects.

themes.name: Are multifactor and ad hoc trademark tests sufficiently predictable and principled for resolving modern disputes?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether fragmented judicial standards adequately define trademark boundaries or should be replaced or supplemented by clearer doctrinal criteria.

themes.name: Do existing statutory and constitutional rules adequately govern trademark registration and restrictions on registered marks?
themes.definition: This question addresses uncertainty surrounding registration, Supreme Court doctrine, and First Amendment limits on Lanham Act provisions governing protected and prohibited marks.

themes.name: Can traditional trademark and intellectual-property categories adequately regulate new digital commercial uses of brands, names, data, and goods?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing doctrines can handle Internet-based services, immersive media, online distribution, and other technologically transformed commercial practices.

themes.name: Which institutions and procedures should determine the scope and enforcement of trademark rights in emerging markets?
themes.definition: This question compares the roles of courts, legislatures, private governing organizations, registration systems, and litigation procedures in producing reliable and legitimate trademark outcomes.

themes.name: Should trademark protection remain limited to preventing source or affiliation confusion?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark law should protect only consumers' ability to identify product source or should also protect broader brand meanings, goodwill, investment, or reputation.

themes.name: Does trademark protection against dilution of famous marks require consumer confusion or demonstrated consumer harm?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether blurring and tarnishment claims should be available for nonconfusing uses based merely on a likelihood of harm to a famous mark.

themes.name: When should unauthorized free-riding on a brand's goodwill constitute infringement?
themes.definition: This question asks whether commercial benefits derived from another party's reputation should be unlawful even when the use does not confuse consumers or appropriate the mark directly.

themes.name: How should trademark law protect brand value without creating overbroad proprietary control?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether legal protection for reputational, psychological, or investment-based brand value can be defined narrowly enough to preserve competition and public access.

themes.name: How should trademark rights be balanced against freedom of expression?
themes.definition: This question examines when expressive, artistic, political, cultural, or noncommercial uses of names and marks should prevail over trademark or related intellectual-property claims.

themes.name: Do current trademark doctrines inadequately protect nonmisleading and transformative uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether fair use, artistic-use, First Amendment, and related defenses sufficiently protect speech that incorporates trademarks without falsely suggesting sponsorship.

themes.name: Should commerciality or financial gain determine liability for unauthorized uses of names and marks?
themes.definition: This question asks whether a use should receive reduced protection when it is commercially motivated, or whether commerciality alone is insufficient without confusion, deception, or other material harm.

themes.name: How should courts distinguish unlawful appropriation from protected use of identity-bearing symbols?
themes.definition: This question concerns the doctrinal boundary between misappropriation of a person, persona, or brand and legitimate reference, commentary, parody, news reporting, or cultural expression.

themes.name: Should publicity and appropriation rights protect the commercial value of celebrity identity?
themes.definition: This question examines whether names, images, likenesses, and other persona-related attributes should receive exclusive legal protection against unauthorized commercial exploitation.

themes.name: What limits should apply to legal control over personal identity and persona?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how rights of publicity and related identity-based claims should be constrained to preserve personal autonomy, cultural expression, public interests, and others' freedom to use language.

themes.name: How should likelihood-of-confusion analysis incorporate actual marketplace conditions and consumer behavior?
themes.definition: This question asks whether courts should rely more heavily on empirical evidence, real-world purchasing contexts, consumer sophistication, materiality, and actual confusion.

themes.name: Is the likelihood-of-confusion standard sufficiently clear and consistent?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether existing multifactor tests produce reliable results across courts or require categorical rules, clearer definitions, or legislative reform.

themes.name: Should consumer harm be required for trademark liability beyond the owner's asserted economic injury?
themes.definition: This question examines whether confusion, deception, materiality, or other demonstrable marketplace injury should be necessary before trademark rights can be enforced.

themes.name: Should generic, descriptive, or commonly used terms receive exclusive trademark protection?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether secondary meaning or commercial recognition can justify exclusivity without improperly restricting competitors' truthful use of language and public meanings.

themes.name: When should product features, colors, or trade dress function as source identifiers rather than protectable product attributes?
themes.definition: This question examines how trademark law should distinguish source-signifying visual features from aesthetically or functionally valuable features that competitors must remain free to use.

themes.name: How should trademark law regulate Internet-based names, domains, and commercial uses?
themes.definition: This question asks when online assets or practices perform a source-identifying function and whether traditional trademark doctrines can be applied without overextending protection to new digital contexts.

themes.name: Do expanded trademark rights produce anticompetitive effects?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether broad control over marks, language, product attributes, or brand associations restricts consumer choice, intrabrand or interbrand competition, and market entry.

themes.name: What legal safeguards can prevent trademark bullying and overbroad enforcement?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether injunction standards, litigation procedures, fee rules, defenses, disclaimers, and other mechanisms can reduce the expressive and economic costs of disproportionate trademark claims.

themes.name: Should trademark remedies be available before actual marketplace harm occurs?
themes.definition: This question examines the justification and limits of preliminary or injunctive relief based on likely future confusion, dilution, or reputational injury rather than demonstrated harm.

themes.name: How should trademark rights operate across jurisdictions and between registered and unregistered marks?
themes.definition: This question addresses territorial conflicts, international and regional regimes, common-law rights, registration consequences, and whether equivalent substantive limits should apply across legal statuses.

themes.name: Should trademark infringement require materially significant consumer confusion rather than abstract or hypothetical confusion?
themes.definition: This question examines whether consumer confusion should remain the central boundary of trademark liability and whether speculative confusion, search costs, or weak associations are sufficient to justify enforcement.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect product attributes and advertising meanings in addition to product source?
themes.definition: This question asks whether trademark and advertising law should address misleading claims about qualities, characteristics, or symbolic meanings rather than limiting protection to source-identifying information.

themes.name: When should nonconfusing third-party uses of trademarks be legally permissible?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the boundary between actionable trademark use and lawful comparative, referential, descriptive, nominative, parody, or otherwise non-source-indicating use.

themes.name: Should famous trademarks receive protection against dilution or diversion without proof of consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether fame, reputation, or consumer attraction justifies enhanced protection against nonconfusing uses, including blurring, tarnishment, and online redirection.

themes.name: Does expansive protection for famous and luxury brands create unjustified market power?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether enhanced protection for strong, famous, or luxury marks restricts lawful copying, comparative use, market entry, and competition beyond what consumer protection requires.

themes.name: Should trademark law remain tied to source identification rather than operate as a general property right in commercial meaning?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark protection may legitimately cover goodwill, attraction, connotation, or reputation when those values are not directly connected to identifying product source.

themes.name: How should trademark rights be balanced against First Amendment protection for expressive works?
themes.definition: This question concerns when films, books, art, commentary, criticism, parody, and other expressive works that use trademarks should be shielded from Lanham Act liability.

themes.name: Should commerciality or financial gain determine whether expressive uses of trademarks or identities are actionable?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether a use’s commercial context should outweigh its expressive character when courts distinguish protected speech from unauthorized exploitation.

themes.name: What constitutional limits should govern right-of-publicity claims involving expressive or media-related uses of identity?
themes.definition: This question asks how state publicity rights should be reconciled with free-expression protections when a person’s name, image, likeness, or persona appears in expressive works.

themes.name: Is the right of publicity a property interest in personal identity or a narrower protection against commercial appropriation?
themes.definition: This question examines whether publicity law should treat identity as an autonomous transferable asset or instead limit protection to economic, dignitary, or unfair-competition harms.

themes.name: When should unauthorized commercial uses of a person’s identity be legally actionable?
themes.definition: This question addresses the roles of consent, appropriation, endorsement implications, reputational harm, and commercial exploitation in determining liability for uses of names, images, or likenesses.

themes.name: Do trademark and publicity doctrines overlap in ways that require separate or unified tests?
themes.definition: This question investigates the relationship between false endorsement, trademark protection, publicity rights, and other identity-based claims when a use suggests affiliation or exploits personal recognition.

themes.name: Are traditional trademark doctrines adequate for Internet-based uses such as keyword advertising, criticism, and domain names?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether existing Lanham Act rules can address online confusion and appropriation without suppressing legitimate communication or imposing excessive control over digital spaces.

themes.name: Should trademark owners be able to control domain names and online practices that divert or redirect consumers without proving source confusion?
themes.definition: This question examines the limits of online enforcement against domains, search advertising, and digital redirection that may exploit brand recognition but do not necessarily misidentify product source.

themes.name: How should trademark law regulate emerging forms of branding and unconventional marks?
themes.definition: This question asks whether categorical registration and infringement rules adequately address nontraditional designations, new commercial actors, brand extensions, and evolving forms of commercial identity.

themes.name: Should recognizable visual or aesthetic features receive trademark or trade-dress protection against copying?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when commercially valuable designs, appearances, or aesthetic features function as protected source indicators rather than as unprotectable product features or material for competition.

themes.name: Do trademark and trade-dress rights improperly restrict lawful copying and intrabrand competition?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether expansive protection of product appearance, brand extensions, and commercial identifiers produces anticompetitive effects or limits consumer access and market entry.

themes.name: How should fair use, exhaustion, and first-sale principles limit trademark-owner control?
themes.definition: This question examines whether downstream resale, comparative use, repair, commentary, and other lawful activities should remain available despite an owner’s claims over a mark or branded product.

themes.name: Does trademark law create excessive private control over descriptive, commonly used, or publicly shared language?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether trademark enforcement converts ordinary words, symbols, or shared meanings into private monopolies and thereby restricts public communication and competition.

themes.name: How should trademark administration and litigation balance enforceability against uncertainty and public interests?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether registration standards, evidentiary burdens, surveys, judicial tests, licensing rules, and enforcement mechanisms provide clear and consistent protection without overreaching against lawful users.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect brand value, goodwill, or persuasive meaning even when consumers are unlikely to be confused about source?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark rights should extend from source identification to the protection of advertising value, reputation, association, or other commercially valuable meanings.

themes.name: Should source identification take priority over trademarks’ quality-signaling, reputational, and informational functions?
themes.definition: This question asks how trademark doctrine should weigh origin identification against the use of marks to communicate quality, reliability, product attributes, or marketplace information.

themes.name: Should consumer perception determine whether a sign functions as a trademark and whether its use is legally actionable?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether actual audience understanding, rather than formal registration or judicial assumptions about consumers, should define trademark meaning and liability.

themes.name: Should trademark liability depend on material purchasing confusion rather than any association or possible misunderstanding?
themes.definition: This question tests whether liability should require confusion that affects consumer decisions or produces meaningful marketplace harm, rather than mere recognition or association with a mark.

themes.name: Should dilution of famous marks require demonstrated blurring or tarnishment harm, or is a likelihood of harm sufficient?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary threshold for federal dilution claims involving nonconfusing uses of famous trademarks.

themes.name: How far should enhanced protection for famous or distinctive marks extend before it becomes an unjustified proprietary right?
themes.definition: This question addresses the fame, distinctiveness, and commercial-strength requirements that should limit expanded protection for well-known marks.

themes.name: When should expressive works, criticism, parody, news, or commentary using trademarks prevail over trademark or dilution claims?
themes.definition: This question examines First Amendment and public-discourse limits on proprietary control over marks used for expression rather than source identification.

themes.name: Do trademark and publicity rights impose unconstitutional content-based restrictions on expressive symbols and information?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether government enforcement or expansion of trademark-related rights improperly discriminates against particular messages or expressive uses.

themes.name: Should the right of publicity protect only a person’s name and likeness, or also broader indicia and commercially recognizable aspects of identity?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether publicity protection may extend to voices, performances, symbols, personas, or other identity-related features beyond literal name or image.

themes.name: When does commercial use of a person’s name or likeness become actionable appropriation rather than permissible descriptive or informational use?
themes.definition: This question seeks a boundary between protecting economically valuable identity and preserving ordinary references, communication, competition, and public access.

themes.name: Should unauthorized uses of a performer’s identity be actionable when they falsely suggest endorsement or affiliation?
themes.definition: This question distinguishes endorsement and affiliation deception from broader claims based solely on unauthorized exploitation of fame.

themes.name: Should trademark and trade-dress protection cover product design, packaging, or other features that communicate qualities rather than source?
themes.definition: This question examines whether product and packaging features should receive exclusive protection when their meaning is functional, descriptive, or attribute-related rather than source-identifying.

themes.name: How should trademark law protect comparative advertising and competitors’ descriptive or informational uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when third-party uses of marks to identify, compare, or describe competing products should be protected from infringement claims.

themes.name: Does aggressive trademark enforcement against imitators and free riders preserve competition, or allow incumbents to obtain excessive market control?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether trademark and unfair-competition claims are being used to suppress legitimate imitation, entry, alternatives, and competitive commercial activity.

themes.name: Should trademark rights be treated as limited, context-dependent entitlements rather than broad property rights in commercially valuable symbols?
themes.definition: This question asks whether trademark ownership should remain confined to legally justified marketplace functions instead of creating general control over a sign or its meanings.

themes.name: How should trademark law allocate protection and liability for marks used in Internet domain names and other cross-border online settings?
themes.definition: This question concerns domain-name dilution, cybersquatting, territorial scope, and the difficulty of applying trademark rules when online uses reach consumers across jurisdictions.

themes.name: Are existing trademark doctrines sufficiently clear and adaptable for technologically transformed marks, digital products, and novel online uses?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether current statutory tests and judicial standards provide predictable limits when digitization changes how marks are displayed, encountered, or commercialized.

themes.name: Who should decide the scope of trademark rights in novel contexts—courts, trademark agencies, online platforms, or private parties?
themes.definition: This question examines institutional responsibility for adapting trademark law and the appropriate constraints on judicial, administrative, platform, and contractual decision-making.

themes.name: Should federal trademark law under Lanham Act § 43(a) reach identity or unfair-competition harms beyond infringement of a protectable U.S. trademark?
themes.definition: This question addresses the statutory and doctrinal limits of extending § 43(a) to claims involving foreign marks, commercial identity, false association, or related harms.

themes.name: How should trademark law reconcile product differentiation and innovation incentives with the patent system’s right to copy and the public domain?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark protection can preserve valuable differentiation without granting perpetual control over product features or undermining competitive copying.

themes.name: Should trademark liability require consequential consumer confusion about a product’s source, sponsorship, or quality?
themes.definition: This question examines whether confusion should remain the central prerequisite for infringement or whether mere association, preference effects, or presumed harm should suffice.

themes.name: How should courts measure consumer confusion when attention, context, and available information vary across markets?
themes.definition: This question concerns how consumers’ sophistication, purchasing circumstances, exposure to information, and communication context should affect findings of confusion.

themes.name: Should consumer perception determine whether an unconventional feature, symbol, or communication functions as a trademark?
themes.definition: This question asks whether actual consumer recognition and source-identifying meaning should control protection for nontraditional marks and branding devices.

themes.name: Should nontraditional trademarks require proof of secondary meaning before receiving protection?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether unconventional product features, appearances, names, or symbols should be protected only after consumers associate them with a particular source.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect brand goodwill and reputation beyond preventing source confusion?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether legally protected goodwill should include reputation, associative value, or brand influence independent of deception about product origin.

themes.name: Should trademark dilution claims protect famous marks from blurring or tarnishment despite the absence of consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question addresses the scope and justification of dilution protection for exceptionally recognized marks when unauthorized use does not mislead consumers about source.

themes.name: How should dilution law balance protection of famous marks against criticism, parody, and other expressive uses?
themes.definition: This question examines whether dilution remedies should be narrowed when the challenged use communicates commentary, cultural meaning, or public-interest criticism.

themes.name: Should individuals control commercially valuable uses of their names, likenesses, or personas as property rights?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether right-of-publicity protection should treat recognizable identity as privately controllable economic property rather than primarily a dignitary or privacy interest.

themes.name: Should the right of publicity be limited when identity is used in expressive, informational, or cultural communication?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when free expression and public access should defeat claims based on unauthorized commercial exploitation of a person’s identity.

themes.name: How should courts resolve conflicts between publicity rights, trademark rights, and copyright in entertainment or expressive products?
themes.definition: This question concerns which intellectual-property regime should govern works that incorporate recognizable people, personas, brands, or identity-bearing material.

themes.name: Should trademark enforcement be restricted when the challenged use is expressive, commemorative, or non-source-identifying?
themes.definition: This question asks whether merchandise, commentary, artistic works, and other communications should receive protection when they use a mark without primarily identifying product origin.

themes.name: What First Amendment safeguards are necessary against trademark claims targeting criticism, parody, and public-interest speech?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing trademark doctrines and remedies adequately prevent private rights from suppressing protected expression.

themes.name: Should trademark law recognize clearer categorical defenses for descriptive, nominative, informational, and other lawful uses?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether explicit limiting rules are preferable to uncertain case-by-case application of fair use and likelihood-of-confusion standards.

themes.name: Do expansive trademark rights improperly restrict competition, product differentiation, and public access to valuable signs?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether control over names, symbols, designs, or associations creates excessive barriers for competitors, entrants, and subsequent users.

themes.name: Should trademark protection be limited when exclusivity creates market power or blocks economically useful third-party uses?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether competition policy and consumer choice should constrain rights whose practical effect is to control market access or branding alternatives.

themes.name: Can the traditional source-identification and search-cost model adequately explain modern brand meanings?
themes.definition: This question asks whether trademark doctrine should recognize symbolic, emotional, cultural, or preference-shaping functions that extend beyond conveying source or quality.

themes.name: How should trademark law treat online uses of marks by nonowners, including domain names and platform-based identifiers?
themes.definition: This question examines whether traditional infringement rules adequately distinguish cybersquatting, competition, commentary, resale, information, and other digital uses.

themes.name: Should trademark owners control noncompetitive or unrelated domain names that incorporate valuable marks?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether domain-name protection should extend beyond likely source confusion and how such expansion affects fair use and free expression.

themes.name: Should trade-dress protection cover product appearance when it overlaps with design or copyright interests?
themes.definition: This question concerns how courts should distinguish source-identifying product features from functional, aesthetic, descriptive, or copyright-protected design elements.

themes.name: Should trademark law impose liability on intermediaries, platforms, or secondary actors for unauthorized uses by others?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when responsibility for trademark-related harm should extend beyond the direct user and how such liability affects digital participation and enforcement.

themes.name: Should trademark institutions and statutory interpretation be reformed to address technological change without creating overbroad property rights?
themes.definition: This question examines whether courts, agencies, and legislatures can adapt Lanham Act doctrine to novel commercial practices while preserving clear limits, competition, and public communication.

themes.name: Should consumer confusion remain the central boundary of trademark infringement?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark liability should generally require confusion about source, sponsorship, affiliation, or quality rather than merely unauthorized use or harm to brand value.

themes.name: How accurately do courts’ assumptions about consumer perception measure actual confusion and trademark meaning?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether judicial presumptions about consumer sophistication, brand familiarity, attachment, and interpretation correspond to empirical marketplace behavior.

themes.name: Should trademarks receive protection for goodwill and symbolic value beyond their source-identifying function?
themes.definition: This question asks whether accumulated reputation, associative meaning, or persuasive brand value should independently justify exclusive rights even without conventional source confusion.

themes.name: Should competitors’ nonconfusing uses of trademarks be legally restricted?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether trademark owners should be able to prevent uses by rivals that do not mislead consumers but may exploit, weaken, or interfere with a mark’s commercial value.

themes.name: Should famous marks be protected against noncompeting uses that dilute their distinctiveness?
themes.definition: This question assesses the justification, limits, and judicial administration of dilution claims involving famous marks used without confusion.

themes.name: How should trademark law distinguish source-identifying marks from descriptive, qualitative, or evocative meanings?
themes.definition: This question concerns the legal tests for separating protectable source significance from ordinary language, product attributes, cultural associations, and other meanings.

themes.name: Should trademark protection extend to nontraditional product features, identities, and commercial identifiers?
themes.definition: This question examines when unconventional marks, product elements, domain names, names, likenesses, or other identity-signifiers should receive trademark-like protection.

themes.name: Do registration, incontestability, and related procedural mechanisms overprotect weak or ineligible marks?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether trademark registration and procedural presumptions create excessive rights that undermine competition, public access, or accurate consumer information.

themes.name: Should trademark rights depend on actual commercial use rather than abstract ownership or priority?
themes.definition: This question asks whether exclusive rights should arise and persist only when a party actively uses a sign to identify goods or services in the marketplace.

themes.name: Does expanding trademark protection create practical monopolies that harm competition and innovation?
themes.definition: This question examines whether broader control over words, symbols, product features, or brand associations raises entry barriers, favors incumbents, or restricts rival innovation.

themes.name: Do trademark enforcement mechanisms structurally favor large established brands over smaller or new market entrants?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether litigation costs, evidentiary presumptions, remedies, and institutional practices distribute trademark power asymmetrically among firms.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect owners’ investments in brand value without demonstrable consumer harm?
themes.definition: This question tests whether investment, reputational injury, or loss of control alone should support liability when consumers are not deceived.

themes.name: How should trademark law protect expressive, communicative, parody, and culturally meaningful uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question addresses when socially valuable speech and cultural expression should prevail over trademark owners’ interests in controlling commercial identifiers.

themes.name: What limits does the First Amendment impose on trademark and right-of-publicity claims?
themes.definition: This question examines how constitutional protection for speech, information, artistic expression, and democratic communication constrains enforcement of identity- and mark-based rights.

themes.name: Should trademark rights be limited when they restrict public-domain language, images, identities, or other commonly usable material?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether exclusive rights over culturally, geographically, generically, or publicly meaningful matter create unjustified barriers to communication and competition.

themes.name: How should trademark law apply to Internet uses, global markets, and digital products?
themes.definition: This question concerns the adaptation of territorial, confusion-based, and source-identification rules to borderless online transactions, digital services, and novel Internet uses.

themes.name: When should Internet intermediaries and other third parties be liable for trademark-related conduct?
themes.definition: This question examines whether hosting, filtering, organizing, advertising, or otherwise facilitating another party’s use of a mark should constitute infringement or trigger remedies.

themes.name: Has the right of publicity expanded beyond a defensible scope of protection for commercially valuable identity?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether state-law protection for names, likenesses, personas, and recognizable identity-signifiers improperly converts fame or public recognition into property.

themes.name: How should publicity rights distinguish a person’s protected identity from representations, associations, and expressive portrayals of that person?
themes.definition: This question addresses the boundary between unauthorized commercial exploitation of identity and lawful use of a persona’s image, attributes, public meaning, or component elements.

themes.name: How should overlapping trademark, publicity, copyright, contract, and other regimes allocate control over identities and expressive works?
themes.definition: This question investigates conflicts among intellectual-property and personality rights, including the role of private agreements and entertainment-industry intermediaries in allocating rights and revenues.

themes.name: Should fragmented multifactor trademark doctrine be replaced with clearer and more evidence-based legal standards?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether judicially selected factors, categorical rules, presumptions, and discretionary remedies provide sufficiently coherent and predictable boundaries for modern trademark disputes.

themes.name: Should trademark protection remain limited primarily to preventing consumer confusion about source, sponsorship, or affiliation?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark law should protect only source-identification interests or also broader interests in brand identity, goodwill, advertising value, and reputation.

themes.name: Is trademark dilution protection justified when a use causes no likelihood of consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether blurring and tarnishment claims should provide famous marks with protection against nonconfusing uses and whether the Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 established appropriate limits.

themes.name: Do expansive trademark rights create excessive control over culturally meaningful symbols and socially valuable expression?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether trademark owners’ control over meanings, associations, and recognizable symbols suppresses reinterpretation, criticism, parody, or other public uses.

themes.name: How should courts distinguish protected expressive uses of marks from regulable commercial speech?
themes.definition: This question concerns the boundary between First Amendment-protected communication and commercial uses that may legitimately be restricted under trademark law.

themes.name: Should noncommercial, noncompeting, or socially beneficial uses of trademarks be categorically protected?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the need for affirmative defenses, safe harbors, or categorical limitations for uses that do not compete with the trademark owner or mislead consumers.

themes.name: Should unauthorized commercial uses of names, likenesses, or personas receive protection under the right of publicity?
themes.definition: This question examines whether individuals should possess property-like control over commercial exploitation of their identities and how such control should be balanced against speech and creative interests.

themes.name: How should publicity claims apply to expressive works that depict, imitate, or simulate real people without reproducing an entire performance?
themes.definition: This question addresses the constitutional and doctrinal treatment of identity-based claims involving films, performances, media depictions, and other expressive works.

themes.name: Does trademark law adequately distinguish source-identifying signs from functional product features and design elements?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether consumer-facing trademark standards can reliably separate protectable product designs or symbols from features whose practical or aesthetic functions make exclusive rights inappropriate.

themes.name: When does product design acquire sufficient consumer-perceived source significance to merit trademark protection?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether consumers perceive product configuration, packaging, or visual design as identifying a particular source and how secondary meaning should be proven.

themes.name: How should trademark law treat descriptive, generic, weak, or widely shared marks?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing distinctiveness and secondary-meaning rules appropriately balance protection of established associations against competitors’ need to use ordinary language.

themes.name: Should competitors retain a right to make truthful, descriptive, comparative, or referential uses of another’s mark?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the limits of trademark control when competitors or users need to identify products, describe qualities, provide comparisons, or communicate useful market information.

themes.name: How should trademark law regulate altered, repaired, modified, or otherwise resold goods bearing another party’s mark?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether use of a mark on goods that no longer originate entirely from the trademark owner creates actionable confusion, and how resale, modification, and consumer information interests should be balanced.

themes.name: Do trademark enforcement mechanisms disproportionately favor famous and established brand owners over competitors and new entrants?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether enforcement costs, presumptions, enhanced protection, and control over valuable identifiers create structural advantages or anticompetitive effects for large firms.

themes.name: Does legal control over famous marks and commercial identities confer undue market power?
themes.definition: This question examines whether expanded protection for highly recognized brands, names, or personas restricts competition, raises entry barriers, or harms consumer choice.

themes.name: Are trademark law’s consumer-search and information-efficiency theories sufficient to justify its scope?
themes.definition: This question tests whether trademarks primarily reduce search costs and communicate consistent quality, or whether current doctrine protects producer investment and proprietary interests beyond those functions.

themes.name: How should consumer perception and marketplace context determine trademark liability?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and doctrinal role of real-world consumer understanding, including likelihood of confusion, endorsement confusion, source recognition, and responses to marks.

themes.name: Are likelihood-of-confusion standards sufficiently predictable and empirically grounded?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether courts apply consumer-confusion tests consistently and whether fact-sensitive evidence should replace uncertain assumptions about marketplace behavior.

themes.name: How should trademark law govern marks and identity-signifiers in Internet search, platforms, and algorithm-mediated navigation?
themes.definition: This question examines liability, responsibility, and limits for online uses involving search results, keywords, domains, platform listings, and algorithmic information environments.

themes.name: Does expansion of domain-name space reduce confusion or instead intensify scarcity and market power over identifiers?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how allocation and expansion of Internet domain names affect trademark owners, competitors, consumer navigation, and control over valuable names.

themes.name: How should trademark law allocate boundaries between trademark, copyright, patent, publicity, unfair competition, and related regimes?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether overlapping intellectual-property and identity-protection doctrines produce gaps, duplication, or unjustified extensions of exclusive rights.

themes.name: Should courts and legislatures reform trademark institutions to constrain doctrinal expansion while preserving reliable consumer signals?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether statutory limits, administrative design, judicial interpretation, and historically grounded reforms can align trademark enforcement with competition, public access, and the system’s stated purposes.

themes.name: Should trademark infringement require that the defendant use the mark as a source identifier?
themes.definition: This question examines whether Lanham Act liability should be limited to uses in which the defendant employs a sign to identify its own goods or services, rather than merely referring to another party’s mark.

themes.name: Should consumer confusion, rather than mere association or diversion, remain the central test for trademark liability?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether confusion affecting consumers’ purchasing decisions should be required instead of liability based on attraction, mental association, initial interest, or reputational harm alone.

themes.name: Should dilution protect famous marks against non-confusing uses?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether famous marks should receive protection against blurring or tarnishment even when consumers are unlikely to believe that the defendant’s goods come from or are affiliated with the mark owner.

themes.name: Should trademark law protect nontraditional marks and product features when that protection may restrict competition?
themes.definition: This question examines how distinctiveness and functionality should limit protection for product designs, features, sounds, colors, trade dress, and other nontraditional commercial identifiers.

themes.name: Should trademark protectability depend primarily on marketplace context and consumer perception rather than categorical classifications?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether courts should rely on evidence of how consumers interpret a mark in actual use instead of formal presumptions about distinctiveness, similarity, or classification.

themes.name: Do descriptive and borderline-distinctiveness marks receive excessive protection through registration or incontestability?
themes.definition: This question asks whether registration doctrines improperly convert weak, descriptive, or otherwise borderline marks into enforceable exclusive rights.

themes.name: Does keyword-triggered or contextual online advertising infringe trademarks?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether search-engine keywords, sponsored links, and other contextual advertising uses create actionable confusion, diversion, or affiliation claims.

themes.name: Can traditional trademark doctrines adequately govern digitally simulated products, services, and environments?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing rules can address trademark uses in virtual environments, user-created digital spaces, and other technologically enabled forms of copying and information mediation.

themes.name: How should trademark enforcement be limited when marks are used for criticism, commentary, politics, or other expressive purposes?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the circumstances in which expressive or noncommercial uses of marks should prevail over claims of confusion, dilution, or reputational injury.

themes.name: Should third-party commercial references to trademarks be protected when they identify, compare, resell, or describe another party’s goods?
themes.definition: This question concerns the boundary between permissible referential, comparative, resale, and luxury-brand uses and actionable commercial exploitation of a trademark.

themes.name: Should the right of publicity be doctrinally distinct from trademark law?
themes.definition: This question asks whether protection for a person’s name, likeness, persona, or identity should require different elements and justifications from protection for source-identifying commercial marks.

themes.name: How should digital media reshape legal control over individuals’ names, likenesses, and identity-signaling attributes?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing privacy, publicity, and personality-rights doctrines adequately address technologically enabled commercial appropriation of personal identity.

themes.name: Should trademark or publicity law prohibit free riding on goodwill without proof of consumer deception?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether the economic value of a mark or persona independently justifies liability for unauthorized appropriation, or whether deception or affiliation must be shown.

themes.name: Has trademark law expanded into unjustified quasi-property rights that burden competition and market entry?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether protection of goodwill, investment, and associative value has exceeded consumer-information justifications and disadvantaged competitors or smaller businesses.

themes.name: Should strong consumer familiarity with a mark narrow rather than expand the owner’s exclusive rights?
themes.definition: This question examines whether highly recognizable marks should face greater limits because familiar words, symbols, and cultural references are especially valuable for public and competitive use.

themes.name: Do expanded trademark and intellectual-property rights unduly restrict the public domain, creative freedom, and cultural communication?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether exclusive control over names, symbols, product attributes, and identities suppresses socially valuable speech, dissemination, imitation, or creative reuse.

themes.name: Does cancellation or denial of trademark registration eliminate underlying protection against unauthorized use?
themes.definition: This question concerns the relationship between federal registration, common-law rights, incontestability, and residual claims when a mark is refused, cancelled, or otherwise ineligible for registration.

themes.name: Should indirect or nontraditional trademark liability be imposed when the defendant has not directly used the mark in an infringing manner?
themes.definition: This question examines whether contributory, vicarious, intermediary, or other indirect theories are justified when the alleged harm results from another actor’s use or from a non-source-identifying practice.

themes.name: Does international harmonization or global supply-chain branding require changes to national trademark limits?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how globalization, cross-border enforcement, and the use of marks to govern global value chains should affect the scope and administration of trademark rights.

themes.name: Should trademark law be justified primarily by consumer information and competition, or also by producer investment and the intrinsic value of marks?
themes.definition: This question compares competing normative foundations for trademark protection, including search-cost reduction, prevention of deception, protection of goodwill, producer incentives, and property-like control.

themes.name: Should trademark infringement require demonstrable, material confusion affecting consumers’ purchasing decisions?
themes.definition: This question examines whether abstract, hypothetical, or merely possible confusion should be insufficient for liability absent evidence that consumers are likely to make mistaken purchasing or affiliation decisions.

themes.name: Should trademark law remain limited to source identification rather than protecting goodwill or brand value as an independent property interest?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether trademark rights should protect only information about commercial source or also control value, reputation, attraction, and goodwill generated by a mark.

themes.name: Should famous marks receive protection against nonconfusing uses on unrelated goods and services?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether owners of strong or famous marks should be able to challenge uses that neither confuse consumers about source nor involve competing products.

themes.name: What level of fame, distinctiveness, and harm should be required for federal trademark dilution protection?
themes.definition: This question concerns the evidentiary and doctrinal thresholds for showing that a use blurs or tarnishes a famous mark’s distinctiveness.

themes.name: Do expansive trademark rights improperly restrict competition, copying, and the public domain?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether broad trademark claims prevent legitimate competitors, follow-on creators, or the public from using common language, symbols, and product features.

themes.name: Should trademark law restrict nonconfusing uses that benefit from a brand’s goodwill without causing demonstrable consumer or producer harm?
themes.definition: This question tests whether free-riding, diversion, attraction, or reputational benefit alone justifies liability when conventional confusion is absent.

themes.name: How should trademark law protect expressive, critical, parodic, and norm-challenging uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question examines the legal boundary between actionable commercial exploitation of a mark and socially valuable speech about, against, or through that mark.

themes.name: Are existing trademark defenses adequate to protect expressive and informational uses against overbroad enforcement?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether fair use, parody, noncommercial-use, and related defenses are sufficiently clear, predictable, fast, and speech-protective.

themes.name: Should the First Amendment limit exclusive rights over identity-bearing commercial symbols and information?
themes.definition: This question concerns how constitutional speech and democratic-information values should constrain trademark or publicity claims involving names, images, performances, and other expressive identifiers.

themes.name: Should personal names, likenesses, performances, and other identity attributes be treated as transferable commercial property?
themes.definition: This question examines whether identity-based interests should be commodified, licensed, inherited, or transferred like conventional intellectual-property rights.

themes.name: What is the proper scope of liability for secondary or unauthorized commercial uses of celebrity identity?
themes.definition: This question addresses when merchandising, advertising, imitation, association, or other uses of a person’s identity create actionable publicity or endorsement claims.

themes.name: Does the transformative-use test adequately protect expressive speech in right-of-publicity disputes?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether transformation provides a workable way to distinguish protected creative expression from unauthorized commercial exploitation of identity.

themes.name: Should trademark protection extend to merchandising and ancillary markets unrelated to the mark owner’s original goods or services?
themes.definition: This question asks whether a mark’s owner should control merchandise, entertainment products, or other extensions into markets where consumers may or may not expect common sponsorship.

themes.name: When should product designs, packaging, colors, or other nonverbal features qualify for trademark protection?
themes.definition: This question examines how source-identifying design features should be distinguished from aesthetic, functional, informational, or commercially valuable features that competitors should remain free to copy.

themes.name: Should nontraditional identifiers receive trademark protection only when marketplace evidence shows source-identifying or associational significance?
themes.definition: This question tests whether sounds, trade dress, digital identifiers, and other unconventional designations should require demonstrated consumer perception rather than formal registration or novelty alone.

themes.name: How should trademark law allocate rights when multiple parties use identical or similar marks in different markets?
themes.definition: This question concerns priority, coexistence, geographic scope, and limits on senior users’ ability to control junior uses that may not create meaningful confusion.

themes.name: May trademark owners use domain-name law to control Internet identifiers used by critics, parodists, or unrelated businesses?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the relationship between trademark rights and domain-name allocation when online identifiers are used for commercial, noncommercial, critical, or parodic purposes.

themes.name: Are traditional trademark doctrines adequate for digital markets, online identifiers, and technologically novel commercial practices?
themes.definition: This question examines whether existing concepts of use, source, confusion, harm, and enforcement can govern Internet-based commercialization and changing information environments.

themes.name: Should trademark rights depend on actual commercial use and consumer perception rather than registration or abstract formal indicators?
themes.definition: This question addresses the relationship between registration, common-law rights, distinctiveness, and real marketplace use in determining substantive protection.

themes.name: How should trademark law respond when a mark becomes generic or loses distinctiveness through widespread public use?
themes.definition: This question examines whether and how legal exclusivity should end when a designation no longer identifies a particular source or retains sufficient distinctiveness.

themes.name: Do fragmented national and international trademark regimes require greater harmonization for globally recognized brands and distributed products?
themes.definition: This question concerns whether divergent jurisdictional rules create unacceptable uncertainty or enforcement gaps and whether coordinated standards would improve regulation.

themes.name: Should courts or legislatures be primarily responsible for defining limits on expanding trademark and publicity rights?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the institutional allocation of authority for resolving emerging claims, setting policy boundaries, and ensuring consistent administration and enforcement.

themes.name: Should trademark liability extend to nonconfusing uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question examines whether uses that do not confuse consumers about source, sponsorship, or affiliation should nevertheless be actionable because they exploit, weaken, or appropriate a mark’s commercial value.

themes.name: When should famous trademarks receive protection against dilution absent consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the legitimacy and doctrinal limits of restricting third-party uses of famous marks that allegedly blur distinctiveness or tarnish reputation without producing ordinary confusion.

themes.name: How should the First Amendment constrain trademark claims involving parody, criticism, and cultural expression?
themes.definition: This question asks when expressive uses of trademarks should be protected speech rather than treated as infringing or misleading commercial uses.

themes.name: Should trademark law prioritize source identification over symbolic and communicative meanings?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether trademark protection should remain focused on identifying commercial source or also cover emotional, cultural, reputational, and identity-based associations.

themes.name: Do current likelihood-of-confusion tests reliably measure consumer perceptions in modern markets?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether judicial tests adequately assess confusion about source, sponsorship, affiliation, or endorsement across different products, consumers, and market conditions.

themes.name: How should consumer sophistication and purchasing context affect trademark-confusion analysis?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts should define consumer care, expertise, purchasing conditions, and other contextual factors when determining whether confusion is likely.

themes.name: Should consumer perception and secondary meaning determine whether a symbol qualifies for trademark protection?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether protection should depend on demonstrated source-identifying significance and acquired consumer association rather than formal registration or the owner’s claimed meaning.

themes.name: How should trademark law treat marks whose meaning depends heavily on context?
themes.definition: This question asks whether the legal scope of protection should vary with the setting, audience, use, and commercial or expressive function through which a mark acquires meaning.

themes.name: Are trademark doctrines adequate for Internet-mediated uses and online markets?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether existing rules properly address domain names, search results, social media, online advertising, platforms, and other technologically mediated uses of marks.

themes.name: Should nontraditional online identifiers receive trademark or unfair-competition protection?
themes.definition: This question examines whether digital usernames, handles, interfaces, virtual identifiers, and other novel signs can satisfy conventional requirements of use, distinctiveness, and source identification.

themes.name: How should trademark law balance brand protection against competition and market entry?
themes.definition: This question evaluates when enforcement protects legitimate goodwill and consumer information versus when it impedes competitors, substitutes, innovation, or entry into a market.

themes.name: Should trademark rights be limited to prevent private control over the public linguistic and cultural commons?
themes.definition: This question asks whether exclusive rights over words, symbols, and culturally meaningful signs should be curtailed when they restrict public communication, truthful reference, or shared expression.

themes.name: How should courts distinguish legitimate brand protection from attempts to preserve incumbent market power?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether doctrinal standards can identify enforcement strategies that use trademark claims to exclude competitors rather than prevent deception or protect source-identifying goodwill.

themes.name: Should the right of publicity be treated as privacy, property, or intellectual property?
themes.definition: This question compares competing theoretical foundations for controlling commercial uses of a person’s name, image, likeness, voice, or other identity attributes.

themes.name: When should the right of publicity restrict unauthorized uses of identity without proof of consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question examines whether commercial value in a persona independently justifies liability or whether publicity claims should require substitution, deception, affiliation, or demonstrable economic harm.

themes.name: How should First Amendment principles limit publicity claims involving expressive works?
themes.definition: This question asks how courts should distinguish protected references, portrayals, and cultural uses of identity from commercial appropriations that warrant liability.

themes.name: Should personal identity and persona be alienable commercial property?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether identity-based rights can be commodified and transferred while adequately protecting autonomy, consent, dignity, and personal interests.

themes.name: How should trademark law regulate protection for aesthetic, symbolic, or associative product features?
themes.definition: This question examines whether features valued for appearance, symbolism, or reputation should receive trademark-like protection when they do not primarily identify commercial source.

themes.name: Do registration systems appropriately allocate trademark rights between formal status and actual commercial use?
themes.definition: This question assesses the relationship between registration, priority based on use, distinctiveness, and substantive entitlement when multiple parties claim rights in the same mark.

themes.name: Are existing trademark defenses and safe harbors sufficient to prevent overbroad liability?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether courts can use context-sensitive defenses, limiting principles, and exceptions to protect truthful information, criticism, competition, and noncommercial expression.

themes.name: How should trademark law govern digital and commercial uses of sports-related identities and content?
themes.definition: This question examines whether sports organizations, athletes, and rights holders may control unauthorized depictions, reproductions, branding, and dissemination without unduly restricting public access and expression.

themes.name: Are privately administered trademark-governance systems sufficiently accountable?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether registration, domain-name, platform, and other private systems allocate trademark-related control transparently and fairly among rights holders, competitors, and the public.

themes.name: How should trademark authority be allocated across federal, state, and transnational legal regimes?
themes.definition: This question examines whether overlapping jurisdictions and conflict-of-laws rules produce coherent protection for marks in cross-border and digitally mediated markets.

themes.name: Should trademark liability turn primarily on consumers’ actual likelihood of confusion rather than on the mere similarity or commercial use of a mark?
themes.definition: This question examines how consumer perception, purchasing sophistication, context, and cognitive biases should determine whether an unauthorized use falsely suggests source, sponsorship, or affiliation.

themes.name: Should trademark protection be limited to uses that function as source identifiers rather than uses that merely invoke a mark’s popularity or symbolic meaning?
themes.definition: This question tests whether advertising, branding, and other ancillary uses should be actionable when they exploit a mark without identifying the source of the user’s own goods or services.

themes.name: Should famous marks receive protection against non-confusing uses that dilute their distinctiveness or damage their reputation?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the justification, statutory limits, and evidentiary standards for anti-dilution protection when consumers are unlikely to believe that the parties are affiliated.

themes.name: Do anti-dilution rules create unjustified trademark monopolies over common language, cultural symbols, or commercially useful meanings?
themes.definition: This question considers whether protection against blurring and tarnishment restricts competition, creativity, and public access more than it preserves legitimate brand value.

themes.name: Should product designs, colors, packaging, sounds, and other nontraditional signs receive trademark protection only when consumers perceive them as indicators of source?
themes.definition: This question addresses how acquired distinctiveness, functionality, consumer perception, and the need to preserve competitors’ access should constrain protection for trade dress and other nontraditional marks.

themes.name: Should trademark law treat keywords, metatags, hidden text, and search advertising as actionable uses of a mark?
themes.definition: This question examines whether Internet-specific promotional uses should create liability when they divert attention or generate advertising value without expressly displaying a confusing source designation.

themes.name: Should famous-mark protection restrict domain names and online redirects that divert consumers even when the domain user disclaims affiliation?
themes.definition: This question evaluates the interaction between dilution, domain-name rules, consumer redirection, and noncommercial or expressive Internet uses.

themes.name: Should the right of publicity be recognized as a distinct commercial property right in a person’s identity?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether names, images, likenesses, and other identity markers embody an economically protectable interest separate from privacy, copyright, trademark, or personal autonomy.

themes.name: To what extent should individuals be permitted to alienate, license, or otherwise transfer rights in their names, images, and likenesses?
themes.definition: This question addresses the limits of commodifying identity while preserving personal control, dignity, agency, and protection against unwanted commercial exploitation.

themes.name: Should the First Amendment protect expressive, artistic, informational, and cultural uses of identities or trademarks against publicity and trademark claims?
themes.definition: This question examines how courts should distinguish protected expression from commercial appropriation and how speech interests should limit exclusive control over recognizable symbols.

themes.name: Should comparative advertising, criticism, parody, and other third-party references to marks be protected when they convey useful market information?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether trademark owners’ goodwill should yield to truthful comparison, commentary, consumer information, and other non-source-identifying communications.

themes.name: Does expansive trademark enforcement improperly restrict competitors’ right to copy functional features, use common language, or enter established markets?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether trademark and unfair-competition doctrines preserve fair competition or instead grant control over product features, designations, and demand that competitors need to operate.

themes.name: Should trademark rights protect marketing-created goodwill and reputational value beyond the information consumers need to identify product source or quality?
themes.definition: This question tests the normative case for treating brands as valuable commercial assets while distinguishing legitimate goodwill protection from an unlimited property right in consumer demand.

themes.name: Should geographic names and origin designations receive exclusive protection when they are also descriptive terms needed by competitors?
themes.definition: This question addresses conflicts between trademarks, geographical indications, descriptive language, producer reputation, and public access to accurate origin information.

themes.name: Should universities, sports organizations, and entertainment performers control merchandising uses of their names, symbols, and performances beyond traditional source-identification claims?
themes.definition: This question examines whether licensing and merchandising rights should extend to educational, athletic, entertainment, or identity-based commercial value without suppressing competition and expression.

themes.name: Are federal trademark-registration standards, including morality-based bars, sufficiently clear and constitutionally valid?
themes.definition: This question evaluates how registration authorities and courts should decide eligibility for legally significant registration rights while avoiding viewpoint discrimination and arbitrary administration.

themes.name: Should trademark remedies and liability depend on bad faith, moral blameworthiness, or the defendant’s actual commercial benefit?
themes.definition: This question considers whether intent should affect infringement findings, damages, injunctions, and the allocation of responsibility for harmful or opportunistic uses.

themes.name: Should courts adopt clearer categorical rules for novel trademark disputes, or should liability remain sensitive to context and competing public interests?
themes.definition: This question examines whether doctrinal predictability is best achieved through bright-line limits or through flexible standards addressing confusion, speech, competition, and market effects.

themes.name: How should responsibility for third-party trademark uses be allocated among platforms, intermediaries, advertisers, and direct users?
themes.definition: This question addresses whether traditional infringement and secondary-liability doctrines adequately govern online marketplaces, search systems, and other intermediated commercial environments.

themes.name: Should intellectual-property law restrict the commercial reuse and dissemination of publicly available information by new digital products?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether existing trademark, publicity, copyright, or related doctrines should protect commercially valuable information while preserving public access, innovation, and lawful reuse.

themes.name: Do overlapping federal, state, trademark, publicity, domain-name, and copyright regimes require harmonization to prevent inconsistent control over the same identity or symbol?
themes.definition: This question investigates whether fragmented legal standards produce conflicting entitlements and whether a more coherent national framework would improve predictability without erasing legitimate state-level protections.

themes.name: Should trademark liability extend to nonconfusing uses of a mark?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark law should impose liability when a use neither misleads consumers about source or sponsorship nor creates conventional marketplace confusion.

themes.name: Does dilution protection give famous marks an unjustified property right independent of consumer confusion?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether blurring and tarnishment claims for famous marks are consistent with trademark law’s consumer-information and competition-based justifications.

themes.name: How should trademark law protect parody, criticism, satire, and other expressive uses of marks?
themes.definition: This question asks when expressive uses should be protected from trademark liability and how courts should reconcile such protection with alleged confusion or reputational harm.

themes.name: Do the First Amendment limits on trademark claims require a context-sensitive rule for expressive and political speech?
themes.definition: This question examines whether content-based control over communicative uses of marks requires heightened constitutional scrutiny or categorical speech protections.

themes.name: When do merchandising uses of names, images, or symbols imply sponsorship rather than communicate information or expression?
themes.definition: This question investigates how courts should distinguish actionable implied endorsement from permissible merchandising, reference, or expressive use.

themes.name: Should individuals have exclusive property-like control over the commercial exploitation of their names, likenesses, and identities?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether commercially valuable identity should receive an independent right of publicity rather than protection only through trademark, privacy, or unfair-competition law.

themes.name: Should publicity rights protect personal autonomy and dignitary interests in addition to economic identity value?
themes.definition: This question asks whether unauthorized uses of identity should be actionable even without demonstrable market substitution, consumer deception, or economic loss.

themes.name: How far should publicity-like protection extend beyond conventional celebrities?
themes.definition: This question examines whether athletes, groups, lesser-known individuals, and other identity holders should receive protection against unauthorized commercial uses comparable to celebrity publicity rights.

themes.name: Should trademark law primarily regulate consumer information or protect accumulated brand property?
themes.definition: This question compares the consumer-confusion rationale for trademark rights with producer-oriented claims to control goodwill, reputation, and intangible brand value.

themes.name: Are consumer confusion and deception sufficient justifications for protecting modern brands?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether contemporary branding practices require protection for symbolic, emotional, or reputational value beyond source identification and misleading commercial use.

themes.name: Should trademark liability require evidence of consequential consumer harm rather than theoretical confusion?
themes.definition: This question asks whether courts should demand empirical evidence that confusion affects consumer decisions, welfare, or marketplace competition before imposing liability.

themes.name: How should consumer perception, sophistication, and marketplace context determine trademark distinctiveness and confusion?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark analysis should rely more heavily on audience characteristics, industry practices, and the communicative context of a mark.

themes.name: Do existing likelihood-of-confusion tests provide reliable standards for emerging and nontraditional trademark uses?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether ad hoc multi-factor tests produce predictable and justified outcomes when marks are used online, artistically, post-sale, or outside ordinary sales contexts.

themes.name: Should trademark doctrine recognize post-sale confusion as an independent basis for liability?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether confusion experienced by observers or later purchasers, rather than the original buyer, constitutes legally cognizable trademark harm.

themes.name: How should trademark law treat unconventional brand identifiers and transformed forms of brand display?
themes.definition: This question asks whether existing registration and infringement categories can adequately protect nontraditional marks, trade dress, and brands presented through new technologies or practices.

themes.name: Should trademark rights be limited when enforcement restricts competition, copying, or market entry?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark protection should yield when it prevents legitimate competitive use, access to unmonopolized features, or entry by new market participants.

themes.name: Do broad and uncertain trademark rights impose disproportionate costs on legitimate users?
themes.definition: This question evaluates whether expansive claims, remedies, and enforcement mechanisms chill lawful commercial, expressive, or informational uses because defendants cannot predict legal boundaries.

themes.name: How should trademark law resolve conflicts among multiple legitimate users of similar marks online?
themes.definition: This question investigates how territoriality, priority, goodwill, platform practices, and Internet-wide accessibility should be balanced when different parties use the same or similar identifier.

themes.name: Do registration, priority, and continuing-use rules fairly allocate trademark rights?
themes.definition: This question examines whether formal priority and use requirements appropriately resolve conflicts between earlier designations, later registrations, and subsequently developed commercial interests.

themes.name: Is statutory or doctrinal reform needed to make trademark and adjacent identity protections coherent?
themes.definition: This question assesses whether fragmented trademark, unfair-competition, publicity, dilution, and secondary-liability doctrines require integrated rules that clarify rights, justifications, and remedies.

themes.name: Should consumer confusion remain the primary boundary of trademark infringement?
themes.definition: This question examines whether trademark liability should generally require a material likelihood that consumers will be confused about source, sponsorship, or affiliation rather than merely an unauthorized use or association.

themes.name: Should trademark owners be able to block uses that create association without causing consumer confusion?
